items.caption:
The best conversations start with a pause.

The small quiet after a question, while the other person decides how much to tell you. Don’t rush to fill it, and the real answer usually comes.

When did a pause change a conversation for you?

Dime con quién andas y te diré quién eres. Inglés: Tell me who you spend time with, and I’ll tell you who you are.

It’s the Spanish cousin of “birds of a feather”. In Spain it’s usually a warning about the company you keep, but friends use it to tease each other too.

Try it with a smile this week, when a friend starts sounding just like their flatmate: “Dime con quién andas y te diré quién eres.”

Who has shaped the way you talk? Tell us below.

items.caption:
Hoy recordamos contando historias. Inglés: Today, we remember by telling stories.

In Spain, 1 November is el Día de Todos los Santos, All Saints’ Day. Families take flowers to the cemetery, and bakeries fill with huesos de santo (little marzipan “saints’ bones”) and buñuelos de viento (light, airy fritters).

In Mexico, el Día de Muertos runs from 1 to 2 November. Families build an ofrenda, an altar with photos, marigolds and the favourite food of the people they miss, and tell their stories out loud.

Whose story would you tell today? Share it below, or tell someone at home.

#diademuertos #todoslossantos #spanishculture #learnspanish #dimemas

Quien tiene boca se equivoca. Inglés: Everyone makes mistakes.

Word for word: whoever has a mouth gets things wrong. It’s what you say when someone mixes up a word and goes red. Nobody speaks without slipping, in any language, so have a go anyway.

Or, as we like to put it: “Equivocarse forma parte de hablar.” Making mistakes is part of speaking.

What’s your favourite mistake in another language? Tell us below.

Hello is where every conversation starts.

World Hello Day began in 1973, when two brothers, Brian and Michael McCormack, wrote to world leaders in seven languages about the importance of talking to each other. The idea: say hello to at least ten people today.

The neighbour, the bus driver, the person you always nod to but never speak to. Who’s first?

Cada maestrillo tiene su librillo. Inglés: Everyone has their own way of doing things.

Word for word: every little teacher has their own little book. You’ll hear it when two people do the same job in completely different ways, and both get there.

We’d put it like this: “Tu forma de aprender es la buena si te funciona.” Your way of learning is the right one if it works for you.

On Friday it’s Día del Maestro in Spain. How do you learn best? Tell us below.
